3.text: rough ice, and allows the snow to cover her over. She is killed in her snow

4.text: den, together with her young, much in the same way as are brown bears in

5.text: more southern latitudes. The polar bear of northeastern Asia is not dangerous,

6.text: and rarely defends itself. When wounded or hunted down, it simply thrusts

7.text: its head into the snow, and waits for the blow.

8.text: Brown bears are occasionally killed by the Reindeer Chukchee, chiefly

9.text: during their winter sleep, because that is the least dangerous method. The

10.text: entrance to the den is sometimes blocked with logs, and the animal is speared

11.text: or shot through a hole made in the roof. The Maritime Chukchee occasion-

12.text: ally have a chance to kill a brown bear, because in the summer-time bears go

13.text: to the tundra far away from the forest border. Thus on the Arctic coast, near

14.text: the Kolyma, brown bears are met on the seashore between the mouth of the

15.text: Kolyma and Brown Bear River (Keiˊñu-weˊem). On the Lower Kolyma brown

16.text: bears even hibernate on the steep banks of some brook, well protected from

17.text: the wind, but beyond the border of the forest. On the Pacific coast I met a

18.text: brown bear in Holy Cross Bay, in June, 1901, that was feeding on seaweed

19.text: along the land-ice piled on the shore.

20.text: On the edge of the forest the Reindeer Chukchee sometimes catch the

21.text: bear with small thin wooden blocks spiked on their upper surface (Fig. 51, b),

22.text: and left on the pathway among fallen leaves. When the bear steps on one

23.text: of these, the spikes penetrate the sole of its foot. A wound of this kind

24.text: rapidly disables it for walking, especially since, in trying to tear away the

25.text: block, the bear only makes the wound worse. This implement seems to have

26.text: been copied from some tribe living within the forest limit, though I am not

27.text: aware that any of the neighboring tribes use it at present.¹

28.text: The Maritime Chukchee catch hares in winter by cornering them and

29.text: finally driving them into a spot surrounded by nets. Women and children

30.text: join in the battue with rattles and sticks to drive the hares in the desired

31.text: direction. I was told that in one successful battue several scores might be

32.text: caught. In times of famine poor families often escape starvation by this kind

34.text: Small animals — like marmots, ground-squirrels, etc. — are caught with

35.text: snares; house-mice, with special mouse-traps; ermines, with a kind of self-acting

36.text: bow (Fig. 52), probably copied from the Russianized natives. It consists of

37.text: a small but strong bow fastened in a vertical position to a wooden frame of

38.text: narrow rectangular shape. The “arrow” is tied at one end to the middle of the

39.text: string, while on its other end is a cross-piece which runs up and down in

40.text: grooves, between the vertical sides of the frame. In stringing the bow, the

41.text: arrow with the attached cross-piece is pulled upward. Then the string is held

42.text: in position by means of a trigger, which is connected by a sinew cord with
